Social Listening · Sentiment Analysis

Airlines Social Listening: From 2015 Complaints to Real-Time Sentiment

Data source: Kaggle — Twitter US Airline Sentiment dataset, combined with an original live-monitoring model
FILE 01 / 06
Power BI · Six Carriers, Jan–Jun 2026

The Question

What actually drives airline sentiment on social media — and is a single company-wide sentiment score even a useful number to report? I combined two datasets on purpose: a historical complaint set and a broader live-monitoring model, to answer both "what do people complain about" and "how is sentiment trending, and why."

The Build

I modeled six carriers (American, Delta, JetBlue, Southwest, Spirit, United) across two fact tables — tweet volume/engagement and topic-level sentiment — sharing common airline and date dimensions. 19 DAX measures cover volume, engagement rate, and sentiment-rate calculations, layered against the original 2015 Kaggle complaint dataset for ground-truth context.

What Surprised Me

The overall net sentiment score was a flat, unremarkable 3.9% — until I broke it out by airline and found a 29-point swing hiding underneath: Delta near +13%, Spirit near -16%. Reporting sentiment as one company-wide average erases the story entirely.

Regional Economics · Tourism

The 100 Year Story: How Theme Parks Built Central Florida's Economy

Data source: Original research — hand-compiled from public attendance reports (Themed Entertainment Association), employment and population records, and park/company histories
FILE 02 / 06
Power BI · 29 Parks, 1924–2024

The Question

In 1924, Central Florida drew about 20,000 visitors a year on orange-blossom rail tours. By 2024, the region drew 79.0 million. I wanted to model what actually built that economy — not just tourism headlines, but the jobs, ticket pricing, and infrastructure behind it.

The Build

I hand-built a dataset covering all 29 theme parks ever opened in the region (19 still open, 10 closed) — attendance, employment, ticket pricing, airport traffic, hotel rooms, and even workforce education programs — across a century. A shared year dimension connects visitor, employment, and population history through roughly 42 DAX measures, driving five dashboard views from park-level detail up to the regional growth story.

What Surprised Me

Since 1971 — when the first major park opened on 27,000 acres of swampland — theme park jobs grew 8.9x while visitors grew only 5.6x. Employment consistently outpaced visitation. This isn't really a service industry; it behaves like a manufacturing line whose only product is experience.

Public Sector · Education Operations

OCPS: Anatomy of a 155-Year-Old District

Data source: Original research — compiled from Orange County Public Schools public data (ocps.net)
FILE 03 / 06
Power BI · District Overview, 1869–2024

The Question

Orange County Public Schools has grown from its 1869 founding into one of the largest school districts in the US — 207,000 students, 214 schools, 23,000 employees, a $3.8B budget. I wanted to know whether a district that size still operates like one organization, or whether it actually behaves like something else entirely underneath the org chart.

The Build

I modeled five operational layers as a connected system: the district overall, individual schools, academic programs, the after-school community-partner network, and the workforce — including Orlando Technical College, a separate workforce-training institution the district also runs. Enrollment history runs from 1869 to 2024, with five dashboard pages covering each layer, all on a custom-built design system rather than a default template.

What Surprised Me

The after-school program isn't run by the district alone — 109 sites are operated by 6 different provider organizations (Boys & Girls Club, the City of Orlando, Orange County Government, the district itself, and others), funded through five distinct channels including a federal grant. A K-12 school system is, in practice, also running a small multi-agency social-services network — and the City of Orlando's own after-school program is larger than the district's internal one.

Retail & Consumer Behavior · Dispenser Analytics

Coca-Cola Freestyle Orlando: The Command Center for 20 Machines, 3 Million Pours

Data source: Locations are real Coca-Cola Freestyle venues in Orlando; the pour volumes, flavor mix, and semantic model are synthetically generated to illustrate the analysis
FILE 04 / 06
Power BI · Command Center, Orlando H1 2026

The Question

Coca-Cola Freestyle machines are built around a signature idea: hundreds of possible flavor combinations from one dispenser. I wanted to know whether customers actually use that customization capability — across 20 real Orlando venues, from sports arenas to hospitals to college campuses.

The Build

I modeled dispenser-level pour data as a star schema — a single FactPours table joined to flavor, location, and date dimensions, with location further split by venue type. A fifth, deliberately disconnected table drives hour-by-hour peak patterns. Five report pages — Command Center, Flavor Universe, Time Intelligence, Marketing Playbook, and an Orlando Sip Map — cover 20 machines, 15 flavors, and six months of pours end to end.

What Surprised Me

Despite the flavor-customization pitch that defines the Freestyle product, 82.9% of all pours are standard "signature" flavors — no mixing at all. The Coca-Cola brand family alone accounts for roughly half of every pour in the network. The feature that defines this product on paper isn't what most people actually use it for.

Executive Reporting · QA & Data Quality

Executive Sales Dashboard: Company Performance at a Glance

Data source: Original research — modeled order-level transaction data for a fictional company, built to illustrate the semantic model and QA process
FILE 05 / 06
Power BI · Company Performance, YTD 2026

The Question

This one started as a standard two-page executive sales suite — revenue, margin, regional and rep performance. The real question turned out to be different: what happens when you actually QA a report before it reaches a C-suite audience, instead of shipping it the moment the visuals look right?

The Build

A textbook star schema — FactOrders connects to customer, product, calendar, and sales-rep dimensions, plus two intentionally unconnected utility tables for DAX measures and refresh timestamps. Two report pages: a daily Company Performance view and a YTD Sales Performance view with a rep leaderboard, customer segments, and a revenue trend.

What Surprised Me

The automated insight text didn't match its own visuals. Page 2 named "Chloe Anderson" as the leaderboard leader while the chart itself showed Marcus Johnson with the longest bar. The same page's Revenue YTD and Profit YTD cards showed "(Blank)" while the insight text separately claimed +18.3% YoY growth. A report can have perfectly correct charts and still mislead a reader through the narrative layered on top of them.

Consumer Products · Platform Growth

Brick by Brick: 75 Years of LEGO's Data-Driven Transformation

Data source: Rebrickable LEGO Database (rebrickable.com) — public catalog data, 1949–2024
FILE 06 / 06
Power BI · Interactive Time Capsule, 1949–2027

The Question

Most LEGO retrospectives are nostalgia pieces. I wanted to know whether 75 years of catalog data actually told a business story — specifically, whether one unchanged core system, the interlocking brick, could explain how the company grew without losing structural coherence.

The Build

I modeled the full public Rebrickable LEGO catalog — 27,069 records across 149 themes, 1949 to 2024 — as a proper star schema: a sets fact table joined to theme, color, and a fully custom date dimension, with bridge tables connecting parts and minifigures. Eight DAX measures on top, including a safely-divided average parts-per-set, power the ribbon, trend, and lifecycle views, plus an interactive year-by-year explorer.

What Surprised Me

LEGO grew from 5 sets in 1949 to 1,339 in a single year by 2025 — expected. What wasn't expected: 7,444 of those 27,069 records, nearly 1 in 3, aren't brick sets at all — they're keychains, bags, and stationery. The real transformation isn't the volume growth. It's that LEGO quietly became a lifestyle-merchandise brand.
